title: free(): invalid pointer: in C++
body_html:
i made the tree data structure, but I have problems when I erase an Object
problem contents below:

* Error in `./t': free(): invalid pointer: 0x00007ffd1df99400 *

중지됨 (core dumped)

Source Code

main.cpp

#include<iostream>
#include"tree.h"
#include"point.h"


using namespace std;

template<class T>
void ShowIntData(Point<T> data)
{
    cout<<data.x<<" "<<data.y<<endl;
}

typedef Point<double> pd;

int main(void)
{
    BTreeNode<pd> bt1; bt1.make();
    BTreeNode<pd> bt2; bt2.make();
    BTreeNode<pd> bt3; bt3.make();
    BTreeNode<pd> bt4; bt4.make();

    bt1.SetData(pd(1,10));
    bt2.SetData(pd(2,20));
    bt3.SetData(pd(3,30));
    bt4.SetData(pd(4,40));

    bt1.MakeLeftSubTree(&bt2);
    bt1.MakeRightSubTree(&bt3);
    bt2.MakeLeftSubTree(&bt4);

    bt1.InorderTraverse(ShowIntData);
    cout<<endl;

    bt1.PreorderTraverse(ShowIntData);
    cout<<endl;

    bt1.PostorderTraverse(ShowIntData);
    cout<<endl;

    bt1.DeleteTree(); // Error occurred
    return 0;
}

events.body_html: Remove delete this line. It does not make sense.

delete must be used only for objects that have been allocated on the heap with new.

In your code all the 4 nodes have been allocated on the stack so calling delete on them is an invalid operation that leads to "undefined behavior".
@bendervader AFAIK it's valid. (One thing that's not valid, though, is calling DeleteTree on a null pointer, but many compilers allow that anyway)
@immibis It's not valid because the object in question was allocated on the stack, not the heap.

@JonathanPotter I mean that delete this; is valid, as long as this was allocated with new. In this case, all but one (per tree) of the objects are allocated with new. The "bug" could be delete this;, or it could equally well be that those objects are stack-allocated.
yes delete should be used only when memory allocated with new
